claims.text: The initial alloy is equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW produced by arc melting and homogenization annealing.
Substituting 5–10 at.% of the NbMoTaW constituents with vanadium will improve room-temperature ductility.
Substituting 5–10 at.% of the NbMoTaW constituents with vanadium will improve irradiation tolerance.
The vanadium-modified alloy will retain BCC structural stability.
The vanadium-modified alloy will retain high-temperature mechanical performance comparable to untreated NbMoTaW up to 1600 °C.
A 5–10 at.% vanadium addition will form a homogeneous BCC phase in NbMoTaW.
The vanadium addition will introduce subtle local lattice distortions.
The local lattice distortions will enhance dislocation mobility.
Features created by the vanadium addition will act as irradiation-defect sinks.
The vanadium addition will alter grain-boundary characteristics and defect-recombination kinetics.
Vanadium is BCC and more ductile at room temperature than the baseline alloy.
Vanadium will lower the critical resolved shear stress and facilitate dislocation glide in NbMoTaW.
Vanadium-induced lattice distortion will enhance atomic diffusion and irradiation-defect recombination.
Enhanced diffusion and defect recombination will reduce helium-bubble accumulation and precursors to irradiation-induced amorphization.
The vanadium-modified alloy will show greater room-temperature plastic strain before fracture than untreated NbMoTaW.
The vanadium-modified alloy will have a lower tendency toward irradiation-induced amorphization than untreated NbMoTaW.
The vanadium-modified alloy will have less helium-induced blistering than untreated NbMoTaW.
Untreated equal-atomic BCC NbMoTaW has poor room-temperature ductility.
The proposed benefits are expected under helium implantation at approximately 400–600 °C and energies around 100 keV–1 MeV.
